**The Imjin War (1592–1598)** | Aspect | Details | |--------|---------| | **Name** | Imjin War (임진왜란) – “Imjin” refers to the Chinese year 1592 (甲辰) in the sexagenary cycle. | | **Belligerents** | • **Japan** – led by Toyotomi Hideyoshi, seeking to conquer Korea and expand influence into China.
• **Joseon Korea** – a tributary state of Ming China, defended its territory.
• **Ming China** – intervened to support Joseon and protect its own borders. | | **Timeline** | • **April 1592** – Japanese forces land at Busan and begin a rapid advance.

• **September 1592** – Battle of Myeongnyang; Yi Sun-sin again defeats Japanese with only 13 ships.
• **Late 1592–1593** – Japanese forces occupy Seoul and the capital region.

• **1597–1598** – Japanese forces retreat; final Japanese withdrawal in 1598. | | **Key Battles** | • **Battle of Hansan (1592)** – naval victory for Korea.
• **Battle of Myeongnyang (1597)** – decisive naval victory with limited resources.
• **Battle of Noryang (1598)** – last major naval engagement; Japanese fleet destroyed. | | **Causes** | • Hideyoshi’s ambition to conquer China via Korea.
• Korea’s strategic position as a gateway to the mainland.
• Japan’s desire to secure tribute and trade routes. | | **Consequences** | • Massive destruction in Korea: cities, temples, and cultural heritage were devastated.

• Increased Chinese influence over Korean affairs. | | **Cultural Impact** | • The war is commemorated in Korean history as a symbol of national resilience.

• The war inspired many works of art, literature, and film. | **Why it matters today** - The Imjin War shaped the geopolitical landscape of East Asia, influencing modern Korea’s national identity and its relationship with Japan and China. - It highlighted the importance of naval power and coastal defense, lessons still relevant for contemporary maritime security.
